mcqs.question: What makes a DP problem fit the '1D sequence' shape rather than needing a 2D table?
options: The input must be an array rather than a string or tree
A single index fully determines each subproblem, and the recurrence reads back only a constant number of earlier indices
The answer must be a count rather than a maximum or minimum
The problem must have exactly two choices at every step
mcqs.explanation: The defining trait is that one index alone describes the state and the recurrence only reaches back a fixed window — that's what keeps it O(n). Needing a second axis (capacity, a second string's position) is what pushes a problem into the 2D shapes covered later in this group.

mcqs.question: In House Robber, why does the recurrence add value[i] to dp[i-2] rather than dp[i-1] when robbing house i?
options: Because dp[i-1] hasn't been computed yet at that point in the loop
Because dp[i-2] is always larger than dp[i-1]
It's a convention with no structural reason — dp[i-1] would work identically
Because robbing house i requires having skipped house i-1, so the best total before house i is whatever was achievable using only the first i-2 houses
mcqs.explanation: Adjacent houses can't both be robbed, so robbing house i forces house i-1 to have been skipped — meaning the prior total can only include houses up to i-2. Using dp[i-1] would incorrectly allow house i-1 to have been robbed too.

mcqs.question: Why does 'always rob every other house starting from house 0' fail as a House Robber strategy?
options: It fails only when the array length is odd
It's not a valid selection at all, since it may rob adjacent houses
A fixed alternating pattern ignores where the largest values actually sit, so it can miss a better selection that skips a different set of houses
It always produces the same result as the correct DP answer, just computed less efficiently
mcqs.explanation: The alternating pattern is a valid non-adjacent selection, but nothing guarantees it's optimal — a large value sitting on an 'excluded' index under that fixed pattern gets left on the table. The DP recurrence considers both options at every position specifically because the best skip pattern depends on the actual values.

mcqs.question: A 1D DP solution gives wrong answers only for inputs of length 2 or 3, but works for longer inputs. What's the most likely cause?
options: An incorrect base case for dp[0] or dp[1] that longer inputs happen to route around or that gets overwritten before it matters
An integer overflow that only triggers on small inputs
The recurrence itself is wrong and coincidentally produces correct results by chance on longer inputs
The loop's time complexity is incorrect
mcqs.explanation: 1D DP bugs concentrate in the first cell or two; a wrong dp[0] or dp[1] corrupts everything built on top of it, but for longer inputs the loop may still 'self-correct' visually or the error becomes proportionally small enough to miss on spot checks, while on tiny inputs the wrong base case is the entire answer.
